name: Expense Fraud
title: Expense Fraud
answer: Expense fraud covers the deliberate misuse of a company's reimbursement process, from inflated receipts and duplicate claims to fictitious vendors, personal purchases dressed as business costs, and collusion between an employee and an approver. It sits inside fraud detection and forensics, where the evidence is usually a stream of claims, receipts, card transactions and approval records rather than a single forged document. The work spans prevention at the point of submission, detection during review or audit, and reconstruction of what happened once a case is opened. Because the amounts are often small and the volume is high, the discipline leans on patterns and outliers rather than on any one suspicious claim.

sections.body: Expense fraud covers the deliberate misuse of a company's reimbursement process, from inflated receipts and duplicate claims to fictitious vendors, personal purchases dressed as business costs, and collusion between an employee and an approver. It sits inside fraud detection and forensics, where the evidence is usually a stream of claims, receipts, card transactions and approval records rather than a single forged document. The work spans prevention at the point of submission, detection during review or audit, and reconstruction of what happened once a case is opened. Because the amounts are often small and the volume is high, the discipline leans on patterns and outliers rather than on any one suspicious claim.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the expense system itself: submitted claims, attached receipts, corporate card feeds, travel booking data, vendor master records and the approval trail that links them. Around that sit the general ledger, HR records for role and reporting line, and policy documents that define what is and is not reimbursable. Analysts typically work in spreadsheets, a business intelligence tool, or a fraud analytics platform that ingests these sources on a schedule. Receipt images and PDFs may pass through optical character recognition so that amounts, dates and merchant names become searchable fields. Access to all of this is usually restricted, because the same data that supports an investigation also contains personal and payment information.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core techniques are rule based tests and anomaly detection. Rules catch known schemes directly, such as a claim submitted twice, a receipt amount above a policy threshold, a round numbered total, or a merchant that appears only for one employee. Statistical and machine learning models look for claims that differ from an employee's own history or from peers in similar roles, which surfaces schemes nobody wrote a rule for. Text and image checks compare what a receipt says against what was claimed, and network analysis maps shared bank accounts, addresses or approvers. Findings are then worked by a person: an analyst pulls the underlying documents, interviews the claimant or approver where policy allows, and writes up the evidence. The output is a case file, not just a score, because a flag alone rarely settles anything.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Expense data is personal data, and in many jurisdictions it carries employment, privacy and payment card obligations that shape what can be collected, how long it is kept and who may see it. Investigations have to respect works council or union agreements, local labor rules and the employee's right to respond, and evidence must be preserved in a way that would survive a disciplinary or legal challenge. Provenance matters throughout: which system produced a record, when it was pulled, and whether it has been altered since. Automated flags are treated as leads rather than conclusions, and a human decision is expected before any adverse action. Vendors supplying analytics or receipt scanning bring their own contracts, data processing terms and security requirements into the picture.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous monitoring rather than periodic audit, with checks running as claims are submitted and feedback reaching the reviewer before payment. Receipt matching is becoming more automated as document understanding improves, which shifts analyst time from data gathering toward judgment and interviews. Generative tools are also lowering the effort needed to fabricate a convincing receipt or supporting email, so detection is increasingly asked to verify authenticity rather than only plausibility. At the same time, tighter privacy rules push toward on device or minimized data processing and toward explainable flags that a reviewer can defend. The practical result is a smaller set of better evidenced cases, with the routine checking handled quietly in the background.
